sla_name: Meaning, branches and connection of Physics
sla_assessment_criteria: Concept of Physics is clearly explained.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Physics is the branch of science that studies matter, energy and the interactions between them in order to explain natural phenomena.
sla_notes_details: The main branches of Physics are mechanics (motion and forces), heat (thermal physics), light (optics), sound, electricity and magnetism, atomic and nuclear physics, and electronics. Physics is connected to other disciplines: it gives chemistry the ideas of energy and atomic structure, supports biology through instruments such as the microscope and X-ray, and underpins engineering, medicine, geography (weather and climate) and mathematics, which is used to express physical laws.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a falling mango is explained by mechanics, the hot sun on a roof by heat, the rainbow after rain by light, and a radio by electricity and electronics.
sla_notes_daily_life: Physics explains everyday things such as why a bicycle stays balanced, how a kettle boils water, how a mobile phone works and why lightning occurs.
sla_exercise: What is Physics?::Physics is the science that studies matter, energy and their interactions.||Name three branches of Physics.::Mechanics, heat and light (also sound, electricity and magnetism, atomic physics, electronics).||Give one link between Physics and medicine.::X-rays and ultrasound scanning use physical principles to see inside the body.

sla_notes_intro: Discoveries in Physics have driven technological, industrial and social development throughout history.
sla_notes_details: Physics has contributed to transport (engines, aircraft, railways), communication (radio, television, telephones, satellites, internet), medicine (X-rays, ultrasound, radiotherapy, laser surgery), energy production (hydropower, solar, nuclear) and industry (machines and automation). Understanding forces and energy also enables the safe design of buildings, roads and bridges.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the study of electromagnetic waves led to mobile phones, while the study of electricity led to lighting, refrigerators and computers.
sla_notes_daily_life: Physics helps people cook with electric stoves, travel by car and plane, communicate by phone and receive treatment using modern hospital equipment.

sla_name: Fundamental and derived physical quantities and SI units
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts of physical quantities are clearly explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Tape measure|Vernier caliper|Stopwatch|Protractor|Beam balance|Magnetic compass|Force gauge
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A physical quantity is a property of an object or event that can be measured; it is expressed as a number together with a unit.
sla_notes_details: Fundamental quantities are independent and are not defined in terms of others: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd). Derived quantities are obtained by combining fundamental quantities: area (m2), volume (m3), density (kg/m3), speed (m/s), acceleration (m/s2), force (newton, N = kg m/s2), pressure (pascal, Pa = N/m2), work and energy (joule, J) and power (watt, W). The International System of Units (SI) is the agreed system of units used worldwide.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the speed of a bus is length divided by time, so its SI unit is metres per second (m/s), a derived unit built from the fundamental units of length and time.
sla_notes_daily_life: Shopkeepers measure mass in kilograms, tailors measure length in metres and drivers read speed and distance, all of which are physical quantities.
sla_exercise: List three fundamental quantities and their SI units.::Length (m), mass (kg) and time (s).||State the SI unit of force in terms of fundamental units.::Newton, N = kg m/s2.||Why is speed a derived quantity?::It is obtained by dividing length (distance) by time.

sla_method: Circle the sage and Questions and answers

sla_teaching_aids: String|Bob|Fixed point|Smooth table surface|Single pulley|Springs|Masses|Online resources

sla_notes_intro: Linear motion is motion of an object along a straight line. It is described using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
sla_notes_details: Distance is the total path length travelled (a scalar, in metres). Displacement is the change in position in a given direction (a vector). Speed is distance travelled per unit time, while velocity is displacement per unit time and includes direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time, a = (v - u)/t, measured in m/s2; negative acceleration is called deceleration. For uniform acceleration the equations v = u + at, s = ut + 1/2 at2 and v2 = u2 + 2as apply.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a car moving from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 seconds has acceleration a = (20 - 0)/10 = 2 m/s2. A runner going around a 400 m track and returning to the start has travelled 400 m but has zero displacement.
sla_notes_daily_life: Drivers monitor speed on a speedometer, and road safety rules on speed limits and braking distance depend on the ideas of velocity and acceleration.
sla_exercise: Differentiate distance from displacement.::Distance is the total length of path travelled (scalar); displacement is the straight-line change in position with direction (vector).||A car increases its velocity from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s. Find its acceleration.::a = (25 - 5)/4 = 5 m/s2.||Give the SI unit of velocity.::Metres per second (m/s).

sla_notes_intro: Force, density, pressure, work, power and energy are key mechanical quantities used to describe how objects behave and interact.
sla_notes_details: Force is a push or pull that can change the shape, speed or direction of an object (unit newton, F = ma). Density is mass per unit volume, rho = m/V (kg/m3). Pressure is force per unit area, P = F/A (Pa); in a liquid P = h rho g. Work is force times distance moved in the direction of the force, W = Fd (joule). Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t (watt). Energy is the ability to do work; kinetic energy = 1/2 mv2 and potential energy = mgh, and energy is conserved: it changes from one form to another but is neither created nor destroyed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, lifting a 10 kg sack through 2 m does work W = mgd = 10 x 10 x 2 = 200 J. If this takes 4 s the power is 200/4 = 50 W.
sla_notes_daily_life: A sharp knife cuts easily because the same force acts on a small area giving high pressure, while a wide tractor tyre reduces pressure on soft ground.
sla_exercise: State the formula and unit of pressure.::P = F/A, measured in pascals (Pa).||Calculate the density of a block of mass 500 g and volume 250 cm3.::Density = 500/250 = 2 g/cm3.||A force of 40 N moves an object 3 m in its own direction. Find the work done.::W = 40 x 3 = 120 J.

sla_teaching_aids: Water tank|Sinking objects|Worksheets|Stone|Dry wood|Picture of floating|Online resources
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Whether an object sinks or floats in a fluid depends on the relationship between its density and the density of the fluid.
sla_notes_details: An object floats if its average density is less than the density of the fluid and sinks if its density is greater. If the densities are equal, the object stays suspended. This is explained by upthrust (buoyant force): an object in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes principle). A floating object displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight. A steel ship floats because its hollow shape gives it a low average density.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a piece of dry wood (density about 600 kg/m3) floats on water (1000 kg/m3), while a stone (about 2500 kg/m3) sinks. Adding salt to water raises its density and makes an egg float.
sla_notes_daily_life: Fishermen rely on boats floating, swimmers float more easily in the sea than in a river, and submarines and hydrometers work by controlling or measuring density.
sla_exercise: Why does a piece of wood float on water?::Its density is less than the density of water.||State Archimedes principle.::An object in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.||Why does a steel ship float although steel is denser than water?::The ship is hollow so its average density is less than that of water.

sla_notes_intro: Mechanical properties describe how materials respond to forces and energy, and include elasticity, hardness, strength and the behaviour of solids, liquids and gases.
sla_notes_details: Elasticity is the ability of a material to return to its original shape after a deforming force is removed. Hooke's law states that the extension of an elastic material is directly proportional to the applied force, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded (F = ke). Beyond the elastic limit the material is permanently deformed. Other properties include tensile strength, hardness, brittleness and ductility. Elastic materials store elastic potential energy, given by 1/2 ke2. The particles of solids, liquids and gases differ in arrangement and movement, which explains their different properties.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a spring that extends 2 cm under a 4 N load will extend 4 cm under an 8 N load, provided the elastic limit is not passed.
sla_notes_daily_life: Springs in vehicle suspensions, rubber bands, bicycle frames and building materials are chosen according to their mechanical properties.
sla_exercise: State Hooke's law.::The extension of an elastic material is directly proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit.||What is meant by elastic limit?::The maximum force beyond which a material does not return to its original shape.||A spring extends by 3 cm under a 6 N load. What load gives an extension of 5 cm?::10 N, since the load is proportional to the extension.

sla_teaching_aids: Online resources|Flow-tube|Thermometers|Stopwatch|Retort stand|Vernier calliper|Steel balls of varying diameters
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Physics uses different instruments to measure quantities accurately, and each instrument is chosen according to the quantity and the precision needed.
sla_notes_details: Length is measured using a metre rule, tape measure, vernier calipers (to 0.1 mm or 0.01 cm) and micrometer screw gauge (to 0.01 mm). Mass is measured with a beam balance or electronic balance, time with a stopwatch, temperature with a thermometer, volume with a measuring cylinder, burette or pipette, and force with a spring balance. Angles are measured with a protractor. Proper use includes avoiding parallax error by reading at eye level, checking for zero error and taking repeated readings.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, to find the diameter of a wire, a micrometer screw gauge is used: main scale reading 1.5 mm plus thimble reading 0.27 mm gives 1.77 mm.
sla_notes_daily_life: Tailors, carpenters, pharmacists, nurses and shopkeepers all use measuring instruments daily, such as tape measures, thermometers and weighing scales.
sla_exercise: Which instrument would you use to measure the diameter of a small wire accurately?::A micrometer screw gauge.||What is parallax error and how can it be avoided?::An error caused by reading a scale from the wrong angle; read with the eye directly in line with the mark.||Name the instrument used to measure force.::Spring balance (force gauge).

learning_activity_name: Relate measuring instruments to physical quantities
sla_name: Relating measuring instruments to physical quantities
sla_assessment_criteria: Precision and accuracy of measurements are clearly related.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Each physical quantity is measured with a suitable instrument, and the quality of a measurement is described by its accuracy and precision.
sla_notes_details: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value, while precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. The smallest division of an instrument gives its least count, which limits precision. Choosing the correct instrument means matching the quantity, the range and the required precision, for example using vernier calipers rather than a metre rule for the thickness of a coin. Errors may be systematic (such as zero error) or random, and they are reduced by calibration and by averaging repeated readings.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, three readings of the length of a pencil, 14.2 cm, 14.3 cm and 14.2 cm, are precise; if the true length is 14.25 cm they are also accurate. The average is 14.23 cm.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pharmacist uses a precise measuring cylinder for medicine doses, while a trader weighing maize needs only a simple scale.
sla_exercise: Differentiate accuracy from precision.::Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other.||What is the least count of an instrument?::The smallest value the instrument can measure.||Match the quantity to its instrument: time, temperature.::Time - stopwatch; temperature - thermometer.

sla_assessment_criteria: The mathematical knowledge is used to describe the relationship between various physical quantities.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Physical laws are expressed as mathematical relationships that let us calculate unknown quantities.
sla_notes_details: Direct proportion (y = kx) applies to F and extension or to mass and weight; inverse proportion (y = k/x) applies to pressure and area for a constant force. Formulae such as v = d/t, a = (v - u)/t, F = ma, rho = m/V and P = F/A are rearranged to make any quantity the subject. Working correctly requires substituting values in consistent SI units, showing the working and stating the unit of the answer. Graphs are used to show relationships between quantities.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, from rho = m/V, the mass of a substance is m = rho V. A 0.002 m3 tank of water (rho = 1000 kg/m3) has mass 1000 x 0.002 = 2 kg.
sla_notes_daily_life: Mathematics in Physics is used by builders estimating loads, drivers estimating travel time and traders using scales and proportions.
sla_exercise: Make m the subject of rho = m/V.::m = rho V.||A car travels 150 km in 2.5 hours. Find its average speed.::v = 150/2.5 = 60 km/h.||A force of 30 N acts on an area of 0.5 m2. Find the pressure.::P = 30/0.5 = 60 Pa.

sla_teaching_aids: Online resources|Small masses|Meter rule|Stop watch|Trolley model calipers|Wooden|Metal rods|Balances|String|Pulley

sla_notes_intro: Experiments help students investigate physical relationships by making observations and measurements under controlled conditions.
sla_notes_details: A scientific investigation involves stating the problem, forming a hypothesis, identifying the variables (independent, dependent and controlled), planning the procedure, collecting results in a table, analysing them and drawing a conclusion. Typical Form I experiments include finding average speed of a trolley on an inclined plane, determining the density of a regular and irregular solid using a ruler and displacement can, verifying Hooke's law with a spring, and finding work and power when climbing stairs. Safety rules must be observed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, to find the density of a stone, measure its mass with a balance, find its volume by water displacement in a measuring cylinder and calculate rho = mass/volume.
sla_notes_daily_life: Simple investigations, such as timing how fast a bicycle moves between two points, help people make informed choices and solve practical problems.
sla_exercise: Name the independent variable in an experiment to verify Hooke's law.::The applied load (force).||How can the volume of an irregular stone be found?::By water displacement in a measuring cylinder.||Why should an experiment be repeated several times?::To reduce random errors and obtain a reliable average.

sla_name: Methods of analysing experimental data (statistical analysis)
sla_method: Group discussion and ICT based approach
sla_assessment_criteria: The methods of analysing experimental data are explained correctly.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Experimental data must be organised and analysed to reveal patterns and support conclusions.
sla_notes_details: Data are recorded in tables with headings and units. Statistical measures include the mean (sum of readings divided by their number), the range (largest minus smallest) and the percentage error. Anomalous readings are identified and excluded or repeated. Averages reduce the effect of random errors, and the spread of readings indicates the reliability of the experiment.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, timing 20 swings of a pendulum three times gives 28.4 s, 28.6 s and 28.5 s; the mean is (28.4 + 28.6 + 28.5)/3 = 28.5 s.
sla_notes_daily_life: Statistical thinking is used when businesses compare sales, farmers compare crop yields and health workers compare temperature readings.
sla_exercise: Define the mean of a set of readings.::The sum of all readings divided by the number of readings.||Find the mean of 12.1, 12.3 and 12.2.::(12.1 + 12.3 + 12.2)/3 = 12.2.||What is an anomalous reading?::A reading that differs greatly from the others and does not fit the pattern.

sla_assessment_criteria: Analytical methods to manipulate experimental data in physics are correctly performed.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Analytical methods allow experimental data to be processed into meaningful results such as averages, ratios and calculated quantities.
sla_notes_details: Raw readings are converted to SI units, substituted into formulae and calculated step by step. Calculated columns may be added to tables, for example velocity from distance and time. Results are given to a suitable number of significant figures, and the percentage error is found as (absolute error/true value) x 100. Uncertainties are estimated from the instrument's least count.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, if a trolley covers 1.20 m in 0.60 s, the calculated velocity is 1.20/0.60 = 2.0 m/s, and this value is written with the unit and appropriate accuracy.
sla_notes_daily_life: Analysing data helps people interpret bills, compare fuel consumption and plan budgets and production.
sla_exercise: Convert 250 g to kilograms.::0.25 kg.||A student measures a true length of 20.0 cm as 19.5 cm. Find the percentage error.::(0.5/20.0) x 100 = 2.5%.||Why should results be written with units?::A number without a unit has no physical meaning.

sla_notes_intro: A graph shows the relationship between two variables clearly and can be used to find unknown values.
sla_notes_details: To draw a graph: choose a suitable scale to use most of the graph paper, plot the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis, label axes with quantities and units, plot points accurately and draw a smooth line or straight line of best fit. The gradient (slope) is found by (change in y)/(change in x). A straight line through the origin shows direct proportion; for a distance-time graph the gradient gives speed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a load-extension graph for a spring is a straight line through the origin; a gradient of 10 N/m tells us the spring constant.
sla_notes_daily_life: Graphs are used in newspapers, weather reports, health charts and business reports to show trends clearly.
sla_exercise: Which variable is plotted on the x-axis?::The independent variable.||What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?::Speed.||What does a straight line through the origin show?::The two quantities are directly proportional.

sla_notes_intro: Reliable conclusions about density, force and pressure depend on careful data collection and analysis.
sla_notes_details: Data on density are collected by measuring mass and volume of samples; data on force by using a spring balance; data on pressure by measuring the force and the contact area, or the depth in a liquid. Results are recorded in tables, means are calculated and compared with accepted values. Sources of error such as parallax, zero error and air bubbles are discussed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a block of mass 0.40 kg and volume 0.0002 m3 has density 0.40/0.0002 = 2000 kg/m3, which can be compared with the accepted value for the material.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers weigh produce, engineers estimate loads and pressure on foundations, and mechanics check tyre pressure.
sla_exercise: How is the density of a liquid found practically?::Measure its mass with a balance and its volume with a measuring cylinder, then divide mass by volume.||Why does a wide base reduce pressure?::Because the same force acts on a larger area.||Name one source of error when measuring volume in a cylinder.::Parallax error from not reading at eye level.

sla_notes_intro: Data analysis is used to explain experimental observations and to test whether they agree with physical principles.
sla_notes_details: Observations such as the constant speed of a trolley on a smooth surface, the increase in speed on a slope, the floating of different objects, or the extension of springs are supported by measured data. The data are tabulated, graphs are plotted and results compared with theory, for example checking that speed = distance/time is constant. Discrepancies are explained by friction, air resistance or instrument limits.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, results showing that the spring extension doubles when the load doubles support Hooke's law.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding why vehicles slow on rough roads or why an object floats helps people make safe choices in transport and boating.
sla_exercise: Why might a trolley on a rough surface show a lower speed than expected?::Friction opposes its motion.||How can data show that two quantities are proportional?::A graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin.||Why should observations be supported by data?::To make conclusions reliable and testable.

sla_notes_intro: A prototype is a working model built to demonstrate a physical principle or solve a practical problem.
sla_notes_details: Development steps are: identify a need, research the relevant principle, sketch the design, select low-cost local materials, construct, test, improve and present. Suitable Form I prototypes include a simple hydrometer to compare liquid densities, a spring balance made from a rubber band and a scale, a hydraulic lift using two syringes, a ship model showing floating and a water-pressure fountain bottle.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a simple hydrometer is made by loading a straw with plasticine so that it floats upright, then marking how deep it sinks in different liquids.
sla_notes_daily_life: Prototype building encourages innovation and self-employment skills, such as making low-cost measuring or lifting devices for the home or a small business.
sla_exercise: Name one prototype that demonstrates pressure in liquids.::A hydraulic lift made from two syringes (or a fountain bottle).||Why should local materials be used in a prototype?::They are cheap, available and encourage innovation.||State the first step in developing a prototype.::Identify a need or problem to solve.

main_competence_name: Apply knowledge of Physics in various contexts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic concepts, theories and principles of Physics
learning_activity_name: Describe the concept and principles of light (sources of light, propagation and transmission, image formation, colours, optical instruments)
sla_name: Concept and principles of light
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles of light are described correctly.
sla_teaching_aids: Torch|Candle|Cardboard with slit|Light emitting diodes|Fluorescent tube
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Light is a form of energy that enables us to see. It travels as electromagnetic waves and can move through a vacuum at about 3 x 10^8 m/s.
sla_notes_details: Sources of light are luminous (the Sun, flames, bulbs) or non-luminous, which are seen only by reflected light. Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation), which explains shadows, the eclipse and the pinhole camera. Materials are transparent, translucent or opaque. Reflection follows the laws: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. Plane mirrors form virtual, upright images the same size as the object and laterally inverted. Refraction is the bending of light when it passes between media of different optical density; a prism splits white light into the colours of the spectrum (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet). Lenses (converging and diverging), the camera, the human eye, the microscope and the telescope are optical instruments.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a rod appears bent in a glass of water because light is refracted as it leaves the water; a convex lens focuses parallel rays onto a principal focus.
sla_notes_daily_life: Mirrors in homes and vehicles, spectacles, cameras, mobile phone lenses and the rainbow all demonstrate the principles of light.
sla_exercise: State the laws of reflection.::The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.||Why does a pencil appear bent in water?::Light is refracted when it passes from water to air.||Name the colours of the spectrum.::Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

main_competence_name: Apply knowledge of Physics in various contexts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic concepts, theories and principles of Physics
learning_activity_name: Describe the concept and principles of magnetism (magnetization and demagnetization, magnetic fields)
sla_name: Concept and principles of magnetism
sla_method: Group discussion and ICT based learning
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles of magnetism are described correctly.
sla_teaching_aids: Different types of magnets|Iron fillings|Card board|Connecting wires|Batteries
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Magnetism is the property of some materials, called magnets, to attract magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
sla_notes_details: A magnet has two poles, north and south; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Magnetic materials are attracted and non-magnetic materials are not. Magnetisation can be done by stroking with a magnet, by an electric current in a coil (electromagnet) or by hammering in the north-south direction; demagnetisation is done by heating, hammering in the east-west direction or by an alternating current. A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a magnetic force is felt, and it is shown by field lines running from north to south outside the magnet. The Earth behaves like a giant magnet, which is why a compass needle points north.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, iron filings sprinkled on card above a bar magnet form a pattern showing the field lines curving from pole to pole.
sla_notes_daily_life: Magnets are used in compasses, fridge doors, loudspeakers, electric motors, door locks and to separate iron from scrap.
sla_exercise: State the law of magnetic poles.::Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.||Name two ways of demagnetising a magnet.::Heating it strongly and hammering it in the east-west direction (or using an alternating current).||How can the magnetic field of a bar magnet be shown?::By sprinkling iron filings on card placed over it, or by plotting with a compass.

main_competence_name: Apply knowledge of Physics in various contexts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic concepts, theories and principles of Physics
learning_activity_name: Explain the concept and principles of static electricity (detection of static charges, types of materials, capacitors, charge distributions and lightning conductor)
sla_name: Concept and principles of static electricity
sla_method: Practical Work and Experiment and Brainstorming
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles of static electricity are clearly explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Small pieces of paper|Plastic comb|Polythene rod|Capacitor|Lighting conductor|Rod|Wires
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Static electricity is the electric charge that builds up on the surface of insulating materials when they are rubbed.
sla_notes_details: Rubbing transfers electrons from one material to another: the material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the one that loses them becomes positively charged. For example, a polythene rod rubbed with wool becomes negative. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charges are detected with a gold-leaf electroscope, whose leaf rises when charged. Conductors allow charge to flow while insulators hold it. A capacitor stores charge, and charge on a pointed conductor is greatest at the sharpest points, which is the principle of the lightning conductor: it safely takes lightning discharge to the ground.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a plastic comb rubbed on dry hair can pick up small pieces of paper because of the charge it acquires.
sla_notes_daily_life: Static electricity explains sparks from synthetic clothes, lightning during storms and why fuel tankers are earthed; lightning conductors protect buildings.
sla_exercise: How does a polythene rod become charged when rubbed with wool?::It gains electrons from the wool and becomes negatively charged.||State the law of electric charges.::Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.||Why are tall buildings fitted with lightning conductors?::To conduct lightning discharge safely to the earth.

main_competence_name: Apply knowledge of Physics in various contexts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic concepts, theories and principles of Physics
learning_activity_name: Describe the concept and laws of current electricity (electromotive force, potential difference, resistance, effect of electric current, domestic electrical installation)
sla_name: Concept and laws of current electricity
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept and laws of current electricity are described correctly.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Current electricity is the flow of electric charge (electrons) through a conductor in a closed circuit.
sla_notes_details: Current I is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t, in amperes. Potential difference (voltage) V is the energy transferred per unit charge, in volts; e.m.f. is the energy given by a source to each coulomb. Resistance R = V/I, in ohms; this is Ohm's law, V = IR, for a conductor at constant temperature. In series circuits the current is the same and R = R1 + R2; in parallel circuits the voltage is the same and 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. The heating effect (P = IV), chemical effect and magnetic effect are effects of current. Domestic wiring uses live, neutral and earth wires, fuses, circuit breakers and switches.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a 12 ohm resistor connected to a 6 V battery draws I = 6/12 = 0.5 A. Two 4 ohm resistors in series give 8 ohms; in parallel they give 2 ohms.
sla_notes_daily_life: Electricity powers lighting, cooking, phones and machines; fuses and earth wires protect people and appliances from overloading and shocks.
sla_exercise: State Ohm's law.::The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it at constant temperature.||Calculate the current when a 24 V supply is connected to a 8 ohm resistor.::I = 24/8 = 3 A.||What is the function of a fuse?::It melts and breaks the circuit when the current becomes too large.

main_competence_name: Apply knowledge of Physics in various contexts

learning_activity_name: Apply mathematical knowledge to describe various relations related to light and current electricity
sla_name: Mathematics in light and current electricity
sla_method: Group discussion and Think ink pair share
sla_assessment_criteria: Mathematical knowledge is applied correctly to describe various relations related to light and current electricity.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Mathematical relations let us calculate image positions, magnification, current, voltage, resistance and power.
sla_notes_details: For light, the laws of reflection give equal angles, and the mirror formula and lens formula relate object distance, image distance and focal length (1/f = 1/u + 1/v); magnification = image distance/object distance. For current electricity, V = IR, Q = It, P = IV, energy E = Pt and the formulae for series and parallel resistors are used. Correct substitution in SI units, showing the working, and giving units are needed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a 60 W lamp on a 240 V supply draws I = P/V = 60/240 = 0.25 A. If it is used for 5 hours, energy = 0.06 kW x 5 h = 0.3 kWh.
sla_notes_daily_life: Electricity bills are calculated using power and time, and opticians use lens calculations when prescribing spectacles.
sla_exercise: A heater draws 5 A from a 230 V supply. Find its power.::P = IV = 5 x 230 = 1150 W.||Find the total resistance of 6 ohm and 3 ohm resistors in parallel.::1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so R = 2 ohms.||A lens has object distance 30 cm and image distance 15 cm. Find the magnification.::M = 15/30 = 0.5.

sla_teaching_aids: Ammeter|Voltmeter|Switch. Meter bridge|Resistor|Connecting wire|Torch|Card board with slits|Triangular prism|Plane mirrors|Curved mirrors
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Experiments in Form II verify the laws of reflection and refraction and the behaviour of charge, magnets and electric circuits.
sla_notes_details: Common practical activities include verifying the laws of reflection using a plane mirror and pins, tracing rays through a glass block and a prism, finding the focal length of a converging lens, plotting the magnetic field of a bar magnet, charging objects by rubbing and testing with an electroscope, and verifying Ohm's law by measuring current and voltage across a resistor. Circuits must be connected correctly, with the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel, and safe practice is followed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, to verify Ohm's law, vary the voltage across a resistor, record the current, and plot V against I; a straight line through the origin confirms V = IR and the gradient gives R.
sla_notes_daily_life: Practical skills help students install simple lighting, repair small appliances safely and use magnets and lenses in daily tasks.
sla_exercise: How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?::In series with the component.||How is the focal length of a converging lens found simply?::By focusing a distant object such as a window onto a screen and measuring the lens-to-screen distance.||What graph is plotted to verify Ohm's law?::A graph of voltage against current, giving a straight line through the origin.

sla_notes_intro: A spreadsheet is a computer program that organises data in rows and columns and performs calculations automatically.
sla_notes_details: Experimental readings are typed into cells and formulae are entered, such as =B2/C2 to find resistance, or =AVERAGE(B2:B6) to find a mean. Formulae can be copied down a column, and charts such as scatter graphs are created from the table. Data must be entered with correct headings and units, and the results checked for errors. Spreadsheets save time and reduce calculation mistakes.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, voltage values in column A and current values in column B give resistance in column C with the formula =A2/B2, and a scatter chart of A against B shows the Ohm's law line.
sla_notes_daily_life: Spreadsheets are used by shopkeepers, farmers, teachers and offices to keep records and calculate totals and averages.
sla_exercise: What formula in a spreadsheet finds the mean of cells B2 to B6?::=AVERAGE(B2:B6).||Name one advantage of using a spreadsheet for data.::It calculates quickly and accurately and can draw graphs automatically.||What chart type is best for showing the relationship between voltage and current?::A scatter (XY) chart.

sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Graphs help identify how one variable changes with another and let students find constants from the shape and slope of a line.
sla_notes_details: A straight line through the origin means direct proportion; the gradient gives the constant, for example R from a V-I graph. A curve sloping downward may show inverse proportion, and plotting against 1/x can convert it to a straight line. The intercept and area under a graph can also carry physical meaning. Students choose scales, label axes with units, draw the line of best fit and use the gradient triangle to calculate the slope.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a V-I graph for a resistor passes through (0 A, 0 V) and (0.5 A, 6 V); the gradient is 6/0.5 = 12 ohms, which is the resistance.
sla_notes_daily_life: Graphs are used in energy meters, temperature charts and business trends to make quick decisions.
sla_exercise: What does the gradient of a V-I graph give?::The resistance.||What shape does a graph of direct proportion have?::A straight line through the origin.||How can an inverse relationship be turned into a straight line graph?::By plotting the quantity against the reciprocal of the other quantity.

sla_notes_intro: Oral communication of results allows students to explain what they did, found and concluded, in a clear and logical order.
sla_notes_details: A good oral presentation states the aim, describes the apparatus and method briefly, presents the results using tables or graphs, explains the analysis, gives the conclusion and mentions sources of error. Speakers use clear language, correct scientific terms, suitable pace and visual aids, and respond to questions politely. Listeners give feedback on clarity and accuracy.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a group presenting Ohm's law shows its table, graph and the conclusion that current is proportional to voltage, and explains that small errors came from meter reading.
sla_notes_daily_life: Oral reporting skills help in meetings, business pitches, health education and community discussions.
sla_exercise: What should an oral presentation of an experiment begin with?::The aim of the experiment.||Why are visual aids useful in presentations?::They make the results clearer and easier to understand.||Name one item to include at the end of a presentation.::The conclusion (and possible sources of error).

sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Data on light and electricity are collected through measurement and observation and are analysed to describe physical quantities.
sla_notes_details: Examples include measuring angles of incidence and reflection, the image distance for different object distances, the strength of magnets by the number of pins lifted, the number of charges detected by electroscope divergence, and current and voltage in circuits. Results are tabulated, averaged and compared with theory, and discrepancies are explained.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, angles of incidence of 20, 40 and 60 degrees give reflected angles of about 20, 40 and 60 degrees, confirming the law of reflection.
sla_notes_daily_life: Data collection helps in comparing the brightness of lamps, the power of appliances and the strength of magnets before buying or using them.
sla_exercise: What is expected when measuring the angle of reflection at different incidences?::It should equal the angle of incidence.||How can magnet strength be compared?::By counting the number of pins or paper clips it can lift.||Why should readings be repeated?::To reduce random error and improve reliability.

sla_notes_intro: Experimental observations are explained by analysing the data collected and connecting them to physical laws.
sla_notes_details: Students use recorded results to explain observations, such as why a bulb glows more dimly in a series circuit with two bulbs than with one, why the electroscope leaf falls when touched, why a compass deflects near a magnet, or why the image in a plane mirror is virtual. Conclusions must be supported by evidence, and limitations such as instrument error are noted.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, adding a second identical bulb in series halves the current, so each bulb receives less power and appears dimmer.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding observations helps people troubleshoot simple electrical faults and use magnets and mirrors more effectively.
sla_exercise: Why do bulbs in series glow more dimly than a single bulb?::The total resistance is larger so the current is smaller.||Why does the electroscope leaf fall when touched?::The charge flows to earth through the hand.||What is the role of evidence in a conclusion?::It supports the claim and shows that it is reliable.

sla_notes_details: Possible prototypes include a periscope using two plane mirrors, a pinhole camera, a kaleidoscope, a simple electric bell or electromagnet, a lightning-conductor model, a simple circuit tester or a home-lighting model with switches and fuse. Steps: identify the problem, sketch the design, choose local materials, build, test and improve, then present with an explanation of the principle.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a periscope is made from a box with two mirrors at 45 degrees; light reflects twice, allowing observation over an obstacle.

sla_method: Digital interactive simulations and Practical Work
sla_assessment_criteria: Concepts of waves and laws of motion are correctly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Text books|Inclined plane|Roller Strings|Ripple tank|ICT- facilities|Stroboscope|Tuning forks|Pipes|Sonometer|Resonance tube
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A wave transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter, while Newton's laws explain how forces change the motion of objects.
sla_notes_details: Waves are transverse (particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel, such as water and light waves) or longitudinal (vibrations parallel to travel, such as sound). Wave quantities are amplitude, wavelength, frequency (Hz) and period, with wave speed v = f x wavelength. Waves show reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference. Newton's first law: an object stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant force (inertia). Second law: resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = ma. Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Linear momentum p = mv, and in a closed system total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after (conservation of momentum).
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a wave of frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 2 m travels at v = 5 x 2 = 10 m/s. A 1000 kg car accelerated by a resultant force of 3000 N has acceleration 3 m/s2.
sla_notes_daily_life: Seat belts protect passengers because of inertia, rockets move by action and reaction, and radio and sound waves carry messages every day.
sla_exercise: State Newton's second law of motion.::The resultant force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration, F = ma.||A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m. Find its speed.::v = 50 x 4 = 200 m/s.||Define linear momentum and give its unit.::Momentum is mass times velocity, p = mv, measured in kg m/s.

learning_activity_name: Describe the concept and principles of equilibrium (moment of force, centre of gravity and types of equilibrium)
sla_name: Equilibrium: moment of force, centre of gravity and types of equilibrium
sla_assessment_criteria: Concepts and principles of equilibrium are described correctly.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A body is in equilibrium when the forces and turning effects acting on it are balanced, so it has no change in motion.
sla_notes_details: The moment of a force about a point is the force times the perpendicular distance from the point, in newton metres (Nm). The principle of moments states that, for a body in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments. The centre of gravity is the point where the whole weight of the body appears to act. Equilibrium may be stable (returns when slightly displaced), unstable (moves further away) or neutral (stays in the new position). Stability increases with a low centre of gravity and a wide base.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a 20 N weight placed 0.5 m from the pivot of a seesaw balances a weight of 25 N at 0.4 m on the other side, since 20 x 0.5 = 25 x 0.4 = 10 Nm.
sla_notes_daily_life: Balances, seesaws, cranes with counterweights and tall buses with low centres of gravity apply the principles of equilibrium.
sla_exercise: State the principle of moments.::For a body in equilibrium, the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment about any point.||Why is a bus with a low centre of gravity more stable?::A low centre of gravity makes it harder to topple.||Calculate the moment of a 15 N force at 0.4 m from a pivot.::Moment = 15 x 0.4 = 6 Nm.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic concepts, theories and principles of Physics

sla_name: Concept and laws of friction
sla_assessment_criteria: Concepts and laws of friction are explained clearly.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Friction is the force that opposes relative motion, or attempted motion, between two surfaces in contact.
sla_notes_details: Types of friction are static (before motion begins), sliding (kinetic) and rolling; fluid friction acts in liquids and gases. Laws of friction: friction acts opposite to the direction of motion, it depends on the nature of the surfaces and on the normal reaction, and it is nearly independent of the area of contact. The coefficient of friction is mu = F/R. Friction is useful for walking, braking and gripping, but harmful because it wears parts and wastes energy as heat; it is reduced by lubrication, ball bearings and streamlining, and increased by rough surfaces.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a 20 N block requires 6 N to slide steadily, so mu = 6/20 = 0.3.
sla_notes_daily_life: Tyres, shoe soles and brakes rely on friction, while oil in engines and bicycle chains reduces unwanted friction.
sla_exercise: Name the three main types of friction on solids.::Static, sliding and rolling friction.||State one disadvantage and one advantage of friction.::Disadvantage: wears out machine parts; advantage: allows walking and braking.||Calculate the coefficient of friction if F = 8 N and R = 40 N.::mu = 8/40 = 0.2.

sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A simple machine is a device that makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force.
sla_notes_details: Types include the lever (three classes), pulley, inclined plane, screw jack, wheel and axle and hydraulic press. Mechanical advantage MA = load/effort, velocity ratio VR = distance moved by effort/distance moved by load, and efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100%. No machine is 100% efficient because of friction and the weight of moving parts. The hydraulic press applies Pascal's principle: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a lever with an effort of 50 N lifting a 200 N load has MA = 200/50 = 4; if VR = 5 the efficiency is (4/5) x 100 = 80%.
sla_notes_daily_life: Scissors, wheelbarrows, bottle openers, spades, car jacks and ramps for loading goods are all simple machines used every day.
sla_exercise: Write the formula for mechanical advantage.::MA = load/effort.||A machine has MA 3 and VR 4. Find its efficiency.::Efficiency = (3/4) x 100 = 75%.||Give one example of a class 2 lever.::A wheelbarrow (or a nutcracker).

sla_notes_intro: Mathematical relationships are used to solve numerical problems about waves, motion, forces and machines.
sla_notes_details: Key formulae are v = f x wavelength, F = ma, p = mv, moment = Fd, F = mu R, MA = L/E, VR = d_e/d_l and efficiency = MA/VR x 100. Students rearrange formulae, substitute in SI units and interpret answers. Free-body diagrams help in identifying the forces before calculating.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a 2 kg trolley pushed with 10 N against 4 N of friction has a resultant force of 6 N, so acceleration a = 6/2 = 3 m/s2.
sla_notes_daily_life: Mathematics allows engineers, mechanics and builders to calculate loads, forces and the machines needed.
sla_exercise: Find the acceleration of a 5 kg object acted on by a resultant force of 20 N.::a = 20/5 = 4 m/s2.||A 0.5 kg ball moves at 8 m/s. Find its momentum.::p = 0.5 x 8 = 4 kg m/s.||Make R the subject of F = mu R.::R = F/mu.

sla_name: Types of experimental variables in Physics related to motion
sla_assessment_criteria: Experimental variables are described clearly.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Variables are quantities that can change during an experiment, and identifying them is essential for a fair test.
sla_notes_details: The independent variable is the one deliberately changed; the dependent variable is the one measured in response; controlled variables are kept constant to ensure a fair test. In an experiment on the acceleration of a trolley, the independent variable may be the pulling force, the dependent variable is the acceleration and the mass of the trolley and the surface are controlled. Errors and how to reduce them are also considered.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in an experiment to investigate friction, the independent variable is the load on the block, the dependent variable is the force needed to slide it and the surface is kept the same.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding variables helps in making fair comparisons, such as comparing fuel use of vehicles under the same conditions.
sla_exercise: Define an independent variable.::The variable that the experimenter changes deliberately.||Name the controlled variables in an experiment on trolley acceleration.::Mass of trolley and type of surface, for example.||Why are variables controlled?::To ensure that only one factor affects the result, making the test fair.

sla_notes_intro: Scientific investigations follow a systematic method to test ideas about waves, forces and machines.
sla_notes_details: Examples include using a ripple tank or slinky to study waves, using a ticker-timer or stopwatch to test F = ma with trolleys, verifying the principle of moments with a metre rule pivoted on a knife edge, finding the coefficient of friction with a block on an inclined plane and finding the efficiency of a pulley system. sla_exercise: What apparatus can be used to study waves in water?::A ripple tank.||How can efficiency of a pulley system be found?::Measure load, effort and distances, then compute MA/VR x 100.||What is the aim of the moments experiment?::To verify that clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments in equilibrium.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic concepts, theories and principles of Physics
learning_activity_name: Explore the basic tenets of heat (measurement of temperature, thermal expansion, thermal energy, transfer of thermal energy, measurement of thermal energy, vapour and humidity in relation to air temperature )
sla_name: Basic tenets of heat
sla_assessment_criteria: Concepts of heat are explored appropriately.
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder one because of a temperature difference.
sla_notes_details: Temperature is the degree of hotness measured with thermometers (liquid-in-glass, clinical, thermocouple) on the Celsius and Kelvin scales (T in K = t in degrees C + 273). Solids, liquids and gases expand when heated, which explains gaps in railway lines and the working of thermometers. Thermal energy is transferred by conduction (in solids), convection (in fluids) and radiation (no medium needed). The heat gained or lost is Q = mc(change in temperature), where c is specific heat capacity; latent heat is the energy changing the state without a change in temperature, Q = mL. Vapour pressure and humidity, measured by a hygrometer, are linked to air temperature and weather.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, heating 2 kg of water (c = 4200 J/kg K) by 10 degrees C needs Q = 2 x 4200 x 10 = 84,000 J.
sla_notes_daily_life: Thermal ideas explain cooking, thermos flasks, the design of houses for cool climates, refrigerators and weather changes.
sla_exercise: Name the three methods of heat transfer.::Conduction, convection and radiation.||Calculate the heat needed to raise 0.5 kg of water by 20 degrees C (c = 4200 J/kg K).::Q = 0.5 x 4200 x 20 = 42,000 J.||Convert 27 degrees C to kelvin.::27 + 273 = 300 K.

learning_activity_name: Explore the basic tenets of the physics of the atom (structure of atom and structure nuclear, radioactivity, nuclear radiations, nuclear processes and thermionic emission)
sla_name: Basic tenets of the physics of the atom
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles related to the Physics of the atom are explored appropriately.
sla_teaching_aids: GM counter|Periodic Table|Chart showing radioactive elements
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The atom is the smallest unit of an element that keeps its properties; its nucleus contains protons and neutrons, and electrons move around it.
sla_notes_details: The atomic number Z is the number of protons and the mass number A is the number of protons plus neutrons. Isotopes are atoms with the same Z but different A. Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei, which produce alpha particles (helium nuclei), beta particles (fast electrons) and gamma rays (electromagnetic waves); they differ in penetrating power and ionising ability and are detected with a Geiger-Muller counter. Half-life is the time for half of the radioactive nuclei to decay. Nuclear processes include fission and fusion, releasing large amounts of energy. Thermionic emission is the release of electrons from a heated metal, used in cathode ray tubes.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a sample with half-life 6 hours has 8 g remaining at start; after 12 hours, two half-lives, only 2 g remains.
sla_notes_daily_life: Radioisotopes are used in cancer treatment, food preservation, smoke detectors and carbon dating, while nuclear power stations produce electricity; safe handling is essential.
sla_exercise: Define half-life.::The time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.||Name the three types of nuclear radiation.::Alpha, beta and gamma.||What is the difference between atomic number and mass number?::Atomic number is the number of protons; mass number is protons plus neutrons.

sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts of electronics are described correctly.
sla_teaching_aids: Periodic Table|Online resources|Text books|CRO|Diode|Transistor|AC Voltage Generator|Connecting wires
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Electronics deals with the control of electric current using devices such as semiconductors, diodes and transistors.
sla_notes_details: Semiconductors such as silicon and germanium have conductivity between that of conductors and insulators, and doping produces n-type (extra electrons) and p-type (holes) materials. A p-n junction diode allows current to flow in one direction only and is used for rectification, changing alternating current to direct current. A transistor acts as a switch or an amplifier, with a small base current controlling a larger collector current. An amplifier increases the strength of a signal. A cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO) displays voltage waveforms.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a half-wave rectifier uses a diode to let only the positive half-cycles of AC pass, giving a pulsating direct current.
sla_notes_daily_life: Electronics is found in phones, radios, television, computers, calculators, security alarms and automatic street lights.
sla_exercise: What is the function of a diode?::It allows current to flow in one direction only.||Name two uses of a transistor.::As a switch and as an amplifier.||Name one semiconductor material.::Silicon (or germanium).

sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts of renewable energy are described appropriately.
sla_teaching_aids: Solar panel|Online resources|Charts|Wind mill model|Batteries|Connecting wires|Inverters
sla_references: TET(2023), PHYSICS SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished and do not run out, such as sunlight, water, wind and heat from the Earth.
sla_notes_details: Solar energy is converted to electricity by photovoltaic cells or to heat by solar collectors. Hydropower uses falling water to turn turbines that drive generators. Wind energy uses wind turbines, and geothermal energy uses steam from hot rocks underground. Advantages include low pollution, sustainability and low running costs; disadvantages include high installation cost and dependence on weather or location. Non-renewable sources such as coal and oil are limited and produce greenhouse gases. Tanzania has good potential in hydropower (for example, the Julius Nyerere and Kidatu stations), solar and geothermal energy.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a solar panel of 100 W in 5 hours of sun produces 100 x 5 = 500 Wh (0.5 kWh) of electrical energy.
sla_notes_daily_life: Solar lamps, solar water heaters, small wind pumps and national hydropower stations provide clean energy for homes and industries.
sla_exercise: Name four renewable energy sources.::Solar, hydropower, wind and geothermal.||State one advantage of solar energy.::It is clean, free and does not run out.||What device converts sunlight directly into electricity?::A photovoltaic (solar) cell.

sla_notes_intro: Calculations in these topics use specific formulae and clear working with the correct units.
sla_notes_details: Key relations include Q = mc(change in temperature), Q = mL, T(K) = t(C) + 273, the gas laws where applicable, half-life calculations by repeated halving, efficiency = useful energy out/energy in x 100, and electrical power P = IV, energy E = Pt. Solar and wind calculations use power multiplied by time to find energy.
